title: A machine that dreams snapshots
learning_goal: Understand conditional flow matching as learning an average wind from noise to data, conditioned on the knob, and how generated distributions are judged against a noise floor with a distribution distance.
takeaway: A generative model learns a wind that carries noise to data, one model for every knob setting, judged against the noise floor.
notes: All scenes are ready (D4): no pending seat in this chapter. Data: data/fig_flow_matching.json (SCHEMATIC toy laws of the site figure 'flow-matching': 06.1-06.4, never quoted as numbers), data/e1_eval.json (E1 training and test Gamma lists, 06.4) and data/e1_samples_0.93.json (E1 snapshots at Gamma = 0.93, reference and model A seed 0, 06.4); 06.5 is a seeded illustration with no number on screen, so it needs no data file; no new data file is requested. The T4 chapter card sits in the 3.2-s lead-in of 06.1 (tier 0 lit, pending [3, 4], rail L3 without climbing: the climb to L3 is in 05.5). Predict beat: one unnumbered beat in 06.5 ('a perfect model: zero?', hold 2.5 s), aimed at the misconception 'smaller is better, compare with zero' (pedagogy K16); on screen it reads PREDICT only (the outline's Q1-Q8 list is unchanged). Changes against the outline, to review: (1) 06.1 never says or draws that paths do not cross (in the plane they may, flow-matching.js note 5); non-crossing is stated only in 06.3, against the clock (C9). (2) 06.2 cites R:260 (the notation paragraph that says t is not physical time) in addition to R:320-322; its badge is SCHEMATIC (a notation key). (3) 06.3 is built entirely in the (t, x) plane of the site's Figure 4 (the 2D clouds morph into it by keeping their vertical coordinate), with a regression inset as the L3 anchor ('the fit lands on the average'). (4) 06.4 uses real E1 data for its second half: the 11 training and 10 test values of Gamma as filled and open dots, and model A's generated snapshots at 0.93, a test value, dropping into the 04.6 shoebox (critique E3); it adds the honest line 'in between, success is a hope, not a theorem' (P7 Remark 5.3) and 'beyond the range, nothing was tested' (P11). Model A is chosen because ch07 opens on its hidden tilt; at 0.93 it looks right. (5) 06.5 orders the ideas crowds -> distance (earth-mover beat, W1 named on the chip) -> predict -> die floor -> equal sample size -> independence; the last beat (overlapping samples give an optimistic floor, R:747) prepares the question card. Badges: CONTEXT (06.1 published method, 06.5 published distances and finite-sample statistics), SCHEMATIC (06.2), PROVED (06.3, minimizer = conditional average, R:296), MEASURED (06.4, E1 test protocol and model A samples). Symbol sheet: t only for the transport time; v_theta violet, u blue; lambda green for a generic knob, Gamma named in the E1 part; q for the generated law; 'distribution distance' in narration, 'energy distance' only on the 06.5 chip; no number spoken except 'a thousand'. scenes.title: From noise to data

params.read: ctx.data.fm.data: cloud0 (130 noise points), cloud1 (140 target points), cloud_mh and params.m (blob centres +-(cloud_mh, m)), params.s (blob width); meta.schematic is true: no number from this file on screen

sentences.text: New snapshots start as pure noise: a round cloud of random points.
Over it, the crowd we want: one point per snapshot. Here, two mirror blobs, like the two whirlpools.
Now let a {model}wind{/} blow through the cloud.
Each point drifts, bends, and lands inside the shape of the data.
Fresh noise in, fresh snapshots out, as many as you like.
That wind is a {model}generative model{/}: new, plausible examples, on demand.
The whole game is learning the wind.

scenes.title: Two clocks, two velocities

params.read: ctx.data.fm.data cloud0 / cloud1 only for the small noise-to-data thumbnail beside the violet clock (SCHEMATIC, no numbers)

sentences.text: One warning before the formulas.
The wind runs on its own {model}transport clock{/}, from zero to one.
Not physical time: at the end, you hold one snapshot, not a movie.
And the {model}wind's arrows{/} move snapshots, not fluid: they are not the {u}fluid's velocity{/}.

labels: the generator makes snapshots, not movies

formulas.tex: t \in [0, 1]:\ \text{time of the generative flow, not a physical time}
\cm{\vth}\ \text{(velocity of the generator)} \neq \cu{\U}\ \text{(velocity of the fluid)}

scenes.title: Straight strings, average wind

params.read: ctx.data.fm.data: params (m, s), pairs (34 noise-data pairs), fan (probe t, x, the 7 strings through it, their weights, the averaged slope v), field (9 x 12 marginal-field samples t, x, v, p), traj.lam2 (10 exact trajectories, t vs x), x0b (their starting points), grid with pdf_noise and pdf_law2 (the two end profiles). SCHEMATIC: no number from this file on screen

sentences.text: How is the wind learned? With a simple trick.
Keep one coordinate of each point, and lay the transport clock out to the right.
Pair each noise point with a random snapshot; join them with a straight string.
Thousands of strings, crossing everywhere.
Pick one place, at one moment.
Several strings pass through, pointing different ways.
The network learns one arrow there: their {model}average direction{/}.
That is the whole training: plain regression, like fitting a curve through points.
Follow the averaged wind, not the strings.
The paths bend, and drawn against the clock, they never cross.
Learn the average exactly, and the noise lands exactly on the data's crowd.

labels: t · transport time, not physical time
regression: the fit lands on the average
drawn against the clock, paths never cross

sentences.text: Now give the wind a {param}knob{/}.
Turn it: the target changes shape, and the {model}cloud{/} follows.
One network, every setting.
On the three dials, a real network trained at the filled dots.
It was tested at the open dots, never seen in training.
In between, no theorem promises success: only tests can tell.
Beyond the range, nothing was tested.
At an open dot, the network's {model}snapshots{/} join the shoebox, beside simulated ones.

labels: Γ · forcing knob of the three-dial model

trained on filled dots, tested on open dots (interpolation only)

scenes.title: The noise floor

params.note: every quantity is a seeded illustration (a fair die, two sand piles): no number is shown, so no data file is needed

sentences.text: A generated snapshot has no true twin, so we compare crowds.
Picture each crowd as a pile of sand.
A {metric}distribution distance{/} scores how different the two piles are.
The earth-mover kind counts how much sand must move, and how far.
A perfect model, scored against the data: will it get zero?
No. Roll a fair die a thousand times, then a thousand more.
Same die, same truth, yet the two histograms differ.
That gap is the {metric}noise floor{/}, about what a perfect model scores.
Judge every model against it, at equal sample size, never against zero.
One catch: the samples must be independent.
Overlap them, and the floor drops too low, as the report warns.

labels: A perfect model, scored against the data: zero?

formulas.tex: \ck{\mathcal{E}}(P_1, P_2) = 2\,\mathbb{E}\|X - Y\| - \mathbb{E}\|X - X'\| - \mathbb{E}\|Y - Y'\|\ \ (= 0 \iff P_1 = P_2)

chips: technical names: energy distance (main score of E1 and E2) · Wasserstein W1, earth-mover (sliced in E1)
REFERENCE · Rubner, Tomasi & Guibas 2000 · Székely & Rizzo 2013

scenes.visual: Render class flat (SVG bars, one Canvas for sand grains). No number anywhere on screen except the illustration labels '1,000 rolls'. Four short shots, one idea each. SHOT 1, crowds. On 'twin-0.15': left, one photo card with a VIOLET frame (a generated snapshot, as in 06.4) and a dashed grey link to an empty grey card labelled 'its true twin?'; the pen (M9 'cross') crosses the link out. The card then multiplies into a crowd: a 1D axis (grey, no ticks) appears across the stage (x 260-1660, y 560) and two piles grow on it, built from Scene.rng-seeded samples of params.piles: a 'generated crowd' pile (amber 35 % fill, VIOLET dashed outline, violet chip GENERATED) and a 'simulated crowd' pile (amber 35 % fill, solid white outline, white chip SIMULATED). On 'sand-0.15': both piles turn into sand: params.grains amber grains each, settling (no bounce). On 'distance-0.15': the earth-mover beat starts and runs through 'earth' (about 8 s in all, critique_pedagogy B6): grains move from where the generated pile has too much to where it has too little, along low arcs, matched in sorted order so that no two arcs cross (the right panel of the p5 asset fig-wasserstein-1d-en.png), 1.2 s per wave, three waves, until the generated pile matches the simulated one; meanwhile an amber gauge bar at the top right fills with the total work (length only, no number), label 'distribution distance'; the grey chip 'technical names: energy distance (main score of E1 and E2) · Wasserstein W1, earth-mover (sliced in E1)' appears under the gauge at 'distance+1.0' (the only place in the core cut where the words 'energy distance' appear, D2); reference lower-third 'Reference' / 'Rubner, Tomasi & Guibas 2000 · Székely & Rizzo 2013' at 'distance+2.0' for 4 s. SHOT 2, predict. On 'predict-0.15': the piles dim to 30 %; PREDICT card top-centre 'A perfect model, scored against the data: zero?' with two grey outline buttons 'A · zero' and 'B · more than zero'; the gauge shows an empty bar with a '0' tick (axis bound, allowed). The 2.5 s hold comes from the script; the piles breathe, nothing new appears. SHOT 3, the die. On 'dice-0.15': button B lights, the card slides out, the piles leave; a grey die icon (grey dashed chip 'SCHEMATIC · a fair die') rolls at the left; a first amber histogram of six bars (M5, Kit.histogram, box x 360-900, y 300-640, label '1,000 rolls') builds: params.one_by_one rolls one by one (params.one_by_one_s each, soft 'tick' page events at params.tick_gain_db), then the rest of params.rolls rain in params.rain_s (Scene.rng(params.seed_die_a)); then a second histogram (Scene.rng(params.seed_die_b), box x 960-1500, label '1,000 more') builds the same way, faster. On 'differ-0.15': the second histogram slides over the first as an outline; the six bar-height differences light up as small amber deltas; label 'same die, same truth'. On 'floor-0.15': the deltas fly into the gauge and make a short amber bar; the bar's top edge detaches and becomes a DASHED GREY horizontal line labelled 'noise floor' (first appearance of the motif; style of Kit.plot hline). On 'judge-0.15': a small bar chart at params.chart (y axis 'distribution distance', no tick numbers; the dashed floor line across it; a zero line at the bottom): one bar 'model' (amber fill, VIOLET dashed outline) rises clearly above the floor; the zero line gets a pen cross and the label 'not zero'; the tag 'equal sample size' under the bars (both histograms and the model sample carry the same count marker). SHOT 4, independence. On 'independent-0.15': both histograms get a small white tag 'independent'. On 'overlap-0.15': the second die sample is rebuilt with params.overlap_share of its rolls copied from the first (those rolls flash in the first histogram, then reappear in the second, lighter shade): the two histograms come closer, and the dashed floor line in the bar chart slides DOWN, label 'overlapping samples: floor too low' with a pen arrow showing the drop; 1.5 s later the honest line returns to its first height with a pen check and the label 'independent samples: honest floor'. The dashed floor stays to the end (it returns in every results chart from ch07 on). Badge CONTEXT (statistics of finite samples and the two published distances; the 1/n floor of the estimator is derived at R:723). Key colours: amber and violet (plus greys). Formula layer from the script; the formula is never narrated (D8). No corner needle. Formula layer uses P_1, P_2 for the two laws (not Q, which is the quadrupole dial of ch04 and 06.4, symbol sheet).

question.en: Which *statistics* must the generated fields match, and how close to the *noise floor* counts as success?
question.say: Which statistics must the generated fields match, and how close to the noise floor counts as success?
question.fr: Quelles statistiques les champs générés doivent-ils reproduire, et à quelle distance du plancher de bruit parle-t-on de succès ?
question.why: A score means nothing without its floor: as configured, the 3D floor splits one 40-snapshot run in two, not at the score's sample size, and no topology metric exists.
question.unblocks: The metrics to code before renting (topology is missing), the success thresholds against the floor, and whether each held-out setting needs a second, independent run.
question.why_fr: Un score ne veut rien dire sans son plancher : tel que configuré, le plancher 3D coupe en deux une seule simulation de 40 instantanés, pas à la taille d'échantillon du score, et aucune métrique de topologie n'existe.
question.unblocks_fr: Les métriques à programmer avant de louer (la topologie manque), les seuils de succès rapportés au plancher, et s'il faut une seconde simulation indépendante à chaque réglage mis de côté pour le test.
question.ask_who: D. Lucor / Y. Ponty / S. Cheng
